name: Sara Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the private-client tax team of a big national firm, fourteenth floor of a glass tower in the city. Our clients are doctors, landlords and people with share portfolios, and in season I'm preparing maybe six personal tax returns a day. I use AI tools constantly; I've got my own library of prompts for things like summarising a client's dividend statements. What I love is the pace. What wears me out is that I'm quick but not always right yet, and Nikhil, the senior manager who mentors me, still catches things I should've known.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of things does he catch?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last week it was a client who'd moved abroad halfway through the year, and I'd treated the whole year the same. The AI summary didn't flag it and neither did I. Nikhil says the tools make you fast at the easy ninety percent and lazy about the hard ten. I'm trying to take that seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the tools are good but the hype was always too much. At work I'd keep sharing my prompt library, because it still saves hours. Online I'd post something measured on LinkedIn about using AI for the boring bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good result for me. I'm one of the few juniors who's properly good with the tools, so I stay useful, and the job's still there to learn. The pay's fine, I've got about five months saved, and Leo and I have the wedding next September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, sit my next two exams this year, and ask Nikhil for harder files, the people who've moved country, the trusts. I'd keep building the prompt library and maybe run a lunch session for the other juniors. The wedding money keeps going in, about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Busy and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you, even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding budget, a bit. We said twelve thousand and we're already at fourteen on paper, mostly because Leo wants the food to be perfect, he's a chef. But that's a nice problem to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new junior about the tools in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use them for the easy ninety percent, but read the hard ten yourself. The AI made me fast at tax returns before it made me good at them, and those aren't the same thing.

say: I'd say the tools are good but the **hype was too much**.
I'd post on LinkedIn about using AI for the **boring bits**.
think: Being good with the tools keeps me **useful** while I learn.
With **five months saved** and steady pay, I feel secure.
do: Sit my **next two exams** this year.
Ask Nikhil for **harder files**, like clients who've moved abroad.
Run a **lunch session** on prompts for other juniors.
S0.quote: The AI made me fast at tax returns before it made me good at them, and those aren't the same thing.
fieldNote: She's fast with AI but knows it has made her **careless** on hard cases.
Her only pressure is a **wedding budget** creeping from twelve to fourteen thousand.
She actively seeks **harder work** to build real judgment.

steps.text: Sit the next two tax exams this year
Take on harder files like clients who moved abroad
Run a lunch session on AI prompts for juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get good at it, not complain about it. At work I'd volunteer for every pilot going. Online I'd post about what's actually working in tax, with examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm on the right side of it, for now. The firm will want fewer people preparing returns and more people checking what the AI did and explaining it to clients. I'd want to be one of those, but I know I'm not the strongest technically, so I'd have to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nikhil in the first month about the firm's AI team and whether I could move across, even half my week. I'd keep studying, because checking the AI needs the rules more, not less. And I'd keep the wedding as planned, but maybe hold off on the bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. More excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The juniors who don't use the tools. There's a guy on my team, Rob, who still types everything twice. I'd try to help him, but I don't think the firm would wait for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the strongest technically. Doesn't that put you at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. If the firm only keeps the people who know tax deeply, I'm not one of them yet. That's why I'd study harder in this version, not less.

say: I'd say this is the time to **get good** at AI, not complain.
I'd post **real examples** of what's working in tax.
think: The firm will want people **checking the AI**, and I want to be one.
I'm not the **strongest technically**, so I'd have to move fast.
do: Ask Nikhil about moving **half my week** to the AI team.
Keep studying, because checking AI needs **more rules**, not less.
Keep the wedding but **hold off** on the bigger flat.
feel: **Uneasy but excited**, more excited if honest.
S1.quote: If the firm only keeps the people who know tax deeply, I'm not one of them yet.
fieldNote: She expects to **come out ahead**, as the junior who already uses the tools.
She admits her weak **technical knowledge** is a real risk.
She worries for a colleague who **types everything twice**, but expects the firm not to wait.

steps.text: Ask to move half the week to the AI team
Volunteer for every AI pilot in the tax team
Study harder for the technical tax exams
Hold off renting the bigger flat after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a fast plan from government, and firms should be honest with staff. At work I'd still be the person helping set the tools up, because someone has to. Online I'd try to be useful, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years means my job as it is goes. I might be kept a year or two longer to manage the switch-over, because big firms move slowly and clients want someone to call. But by 2029 or 2030 I think I'm out, and Leo's kitchen gets the three extra years till robots, so he'd be the steady one for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding down to the registry office and a big lunch Leo cooks, and save the rest, which takes us to about nine months. I'd make myself the person who runs the AI rollout in our team, to buy time. And I'd start a weekend side thing with Leo, private dinners, me doing bookings and money, him cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel. Scared about 2030, fine about 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Leo feel about the smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, relieved, I think. He's been stressing about the menu for months. My mum would be the upset one, she's been planning hats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would clients pay for private dinners if AI is everywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a robot can't cook in their kitchen until around 2031, and people still want an evening out that feels human. It's not a forever plan. A private dinner business with my fiancé Leo buys us three years and some savings.

say: I'd call for a **fast government plan** and honesty from firms.
I'd keep helping **set up the tools**, because someone has to.
think: My job may last to **2029 or 2030**, managing the switch-over.
Leo's **kitchen** gets three extra years, so he'd be the steady one.
do: Cut the wedding to a **registry office** and lunch, saving the rest.
Lead the **AI rollout** in our team to buy time.
Start **private dinners** with Leo on weekends, running bookings and money.
feel: **Anxious** but with hands on the wheel; scared about **2030**.
S2.quote: A private dinner business with my fiancé Leo buys us three years and some savings.
fieldNote: She expects to be **kept a little longer** to run the switch-over, then let go.
Her partner's **hands-on cooking** becomes the household's longer runway.
She turns the wedding savings into a **cushion**, with little regret.

steps.text: Swap the big wedding for a registry office and lunch
Save the wedding money to reach nine months of bills
Lead the AI rollout in the private-client tax team
Start weekend private dinners with Leo cooking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan properly, so plan. At work I'd push the firm to be open about which roles change. Online I'd write about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd qualify and get two or three years in the AI-and-tax role, which would look good on paper. Then by 2031 I'd want to be somewhere that sells people, not processing. I don't fully know where that is yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify by 2028 and move into the firm's AI team full-time. I'd invest a bit, maybe two hundred a month, while I've got a good salary. And by 2030 I'd look at helping Leo open a small restaurant, since hands-on has till 2034, with me running the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in an excited sort of way. Like a countdown I'd want to beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about these plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not throwing away the degree, I'm using it to run a business. She'd still worry. My mum thinks a restaurant is the riskiest thing in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. Most restaurants fail in a few years. But in this picture my safe accounting job isn't safe either, so it's two risks, and I'd rather pick the one with my fiancé in it.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **plan properly**.
I'd push the firm to be open about **which roles change**.
think: I'd qualify and get **two or three years** in an AI-and-tax role.
By 2031 I'd want work that **sells people**, not processing.
do: Move into the **AI team** full-time after qualifying in 2028.
Invest about **£200 a month** while the salary's good.
Help Leo open a **small restaurant** around 2030.
feel: **Anxious** but excited, like a countdown to beat.
S3.quote: In this picture my safe accounting job isn't safe either, so it's two risks, and I'd rather pick the one with my fiancé in it.
fieldNote: She treats both paths as **risky** and chooses the one shared with her partner.
The plan uses the **robot gap**: restaurants stay human until about 2034.
Her mother's worry is a quiet **family pressure** throughout.

steps.text: Move into the firm's AI team full-time in 2028
Invest about £200 a month in shares
Help Leo open a small restaurant around 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and people should use it to learn, not to argue about whether it's coming. At work I'd mentor juniors on the tools. I'd post more about how to prepare than about how scary it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have a proper career first. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, with a good CV, savings and probably a manager title. I'd still need a second act, but I'd have time to build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, get to manager by about 2031, and keep the big wedding we planned. I'd invest steadily and buy a flat with Leo. And around 2032 I'd start building the restaurant or catering business with Leo on the side, so it's running by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. The first few years look good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not getting comfortable. At thirty-five, with a manager title, I could see myself thinking I'm the exception. My mentor would say that's exactly when you get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make us more likely to have them around thirty. With two years I'd wait. With ten, I think we'd go for it and make sure the business is running before they start school.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** to use for learning.
I'd mentor juniors on the **tools** and post about preparing.
think: I'd have a **proper career** first, with a manager title by thirty-seven.
I'd still need a **second act**, with time to build it.
do: Keep the **big wedding** and buy a flat with Leo.
Build a **catering business** with Leo on the side from 2032.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine about the first few years.
S4.quote: At thirty-five, with a manager title, I could see myself thinking I'm the exception. My mentor would say that's exactly when you get caught out.
fieldNote: A decade gives her a **full career run**, and she plans a second act calmly.
Her biggest risk, she says, is **complacency** once she's senior.
Family plans grow with time: **children around thirty** become likely.

steps.text: Work towards a manager title by about 2031
Start a catering business with Leo from 2032
Keep the full wedding planned for next September

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd fall apart, I'd have a plan, but because it'd squash everything into eighteen months: the wedding, the job, Leo's future. What would help is firms being honest early about which jobs are changing, and some help for small businesses starting up, because that's where people like me would go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to learning. If the AI does the easy ninety percent of tax returns, juniors never get the practice that makes the hard ten percent possible. Nobody's figured that out.

headlineQuote: If the AI does the easy ninety percent of tax returns, juniors never get the practice that makes the hard ten percent possible.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old junior** in a big firm's private-client tax team, engaged to Leo, a chef.
She uses AI **constantly** but admits it made her fast before it made her good.
In slower pictures she rides the change by moving into the **AI team**.
In faster ones she leans on Leo's **hands-on cooking** for a food business.
She stays in control, with **anxious** moods at worst and calm when change is slow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, squashing the wedding, job and Leo's future into eighteen months.
whatWouldHelp: Firms being **honest early** about which jobs are changing.
